_comment: The pipe telegraph at the pipe-heads in the lane. A slow correspondence in crew code with someone below, one exchange a night. Replies arrive the next Hush (since:tg_sent>=1).

nocode.say: You rap on the pipe-head. The sound goes down and keeps going.
Knocking isn't the hard part. Knowing what to say in pipe is. Barnaby would know.

first.say: The lane is dark. The pipe-heads stand in a row like people waiting for a tram nobody remembers.
You put your knuckles to the cold brass. Three. Two. Three.
It goes down into the ground and doesn't come back. That's how it works, Barnaby said. Answers take the long way. Tomorrow, at Hush.

wait.say: You've knocked tonight already. The pipe hums with Wick's own water and nothing else.
Answers take the long way. Tomorrow.

reply1.say: You haven't lifted your hand yet when the pipe knocks first.
Three. Two. Three. Then two single knocks, close. Then two more.
It sounds like someone who has waited a very long time to say yes to anything.
The question goes down. Somewhere below, someone is going to have to work out how to answer it.

reply2.say: The answer starts before the Hush is properly dark. One knock. A pause. One knock. A pause.
You count them on the pipe with chalk. Twelve. Slow and careful, like someone pointing at faces round a table.
Twelve people. Down there. Eleven years after the valve shut.
The answer is a pattern you don't know: a tap for the row, a tap for the column. Letters. Nobody uses letters, Barnaby said. Letters are for when you've run out of everything else.
You chalk the taps on the pipe-head and work them through twice. P. E. L. L.
Pell. A name. Not a crew name anyone has mentioned.

reply3.say: Letters again, tonight. You've got better at the chalk. P. E. L. L.
Pell. Whoever that is, they were taught the old code by someone who knew it properly.
One knock. A pause. One knock. You count with the chalk. Twelve.
Twelve people, and one of them is called Pell.
You stand in the lane a while with your hand on the brass. It is faintly warm. It wasn't, before.
You knock it twice to be sure. You've stopped feeling silly doing this. That happened sometime around the second night.

reply4.say: Tonight it's fast, and rough, like someone knocking with the flat of a fist.
Then a long pause, and, more slowly, as if to make up for it: three. Two. Three.
You wonder what they think you are. A town? A ghost? A pipe that learned to be lonely?

reply5.say: One answer, and then nothing else all night.
Not 'come up'. Not 'send'. They want someone to come down.
Barnaby needs to hear this, and so does everyone else.

after.say: You knock three-two-three. A moment later, very faintly: three-two-three.
Somebody down there is keeping the pipe company.

after_met.say: You knock three-two-three. The answer comes back almost before you've finished: three-two-three, and then a little flourish nobody taught Pell.
It's the sound of someone grinning.

after_wren.say: The answer takes a long time. When it comes, it's slow, and it's the same as always, and it's Pell's hand, not hers.
